name: cpp-matmul (talhasaruhan)
baseline: Eigen MatrixXd product built with EIGEN_USE_MKL_ALL (so Intel MKL dgemm, 12 threads, TBB), also multithreaded NumPy on MKL
workload: Multithreaded double-precision square matrix-matrix multiplication, one C = A*B timing per run, N up to about 15,000, compared against Eigen with the MKL backend.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Current implementation runs identically or slightly faster than Eigen (MKL+TBB) for all test cases (tested up to N=15K)'. NumPy (MKL) was 'consistently slower than Eigen(MKL+TBB)'. The result is shown only as a graph (Benchmark1.png) and benchmark.xlsx; no ratio is given in the text.
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 2017, x64 Release plus /O2 /Ot /Gy /arch:AVX2 /fp:fast /std:c++17; hand-written AVX/FMA intrinsics, software prefetching, runtime-detected block sizes. The Eigen benchmark (Benchmarks/EigenBenchmark.cpp) defines EIGEN_USE_MKL_ALL and sets 12 threads.
tradeoffs: Windows only (Win32 processor-mapping and thread-affinity calls, cpuid), x86-64 with AVX/FMA only, double-precision square matrices, no BLAS-style API (README says to copy CPUUtils.*, ThreadPool.h and MatrixMul.cpp into a namespace), plain O(N^3) with no Strassen. Block sizes are detected at run time from cache sizes.
caveats: No license file (raw LICENSE, LICENSE.md and LICENSE.txt all 404, repo page shows none), so the code is reference-only. Tier A is assigned because benchmark code (EigenBenchmark.cpp, NumpyBenchmark.py), compiler, flags and CPU are all public, but the numbers exist only as a PNG graph and an xlsx, and the text claim is qualitative ('identically or slightly faster'); a verifier should open the graph and could reasonably re-tier to C. The Eigen/MKL/TBB versions are not stated, and the benchmark times one multiplication with 12 threads on a single desktop CPU. README text is partly stale: it strikes out 'Still a factor of 2 to achieve MKL performance' and also says that on this CPU the build without software prefetching is about 15% faster. Single author, last commit Nov 2018.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'small matrix multiplication library outperforms Intel MKL OpenBLAS Eigen C++ github benchmark blog' listed https://github.com/talhasaruhan/cpp-matmul (title 'cpp matmul'); then opened the repo page, README, Benchmarks folder, EigenBenchmark.cpp and the commit list.

name: Aliaksei Sala C++ GEMM (C++Now 2025 / CppCon 2025 talk)
workload: Dense double-precision square GEMM, 2880 x 2880 row-major std::vector<double> (larger than L3), multithreaded, built up step by step from naive loops to tiled, packed, register-blocked, unrolled and prefetched kernels and compared with OpenBLAS.
claimed_speedup: Slides (opened): final optimised version 142.2 GFLOPS (0.336 s, 96.6% of the 147.2 GFLOPS peak) vs OpenBLAS 154.1 GFLOPS (0.310 s) on the i5-6300HQ, so OpenBLAS is about 8% faster there (derived from page data). A claim that the custom implementation beats OpenBLAS (1.70 TFLOPS vs 1.58 TFLOPS on an AMD Ryzen 9 9950X) comes only from a WebSearch snippet of the author's Medium article (snippet only, page blocked).
compiler_and_flags: Slides: Linux, -O3 -march=haswell -ffast-math; slides say the final kernels are written in assembly and that other versions vary by up to 40% between Clang and GCC (compiler version not stated).
hardware: Intel Core i5-6300HQ (4 cores, 2.3 GHz), Linux, per slides; AMD Ryzen 9 9950X per snippet only
stars_or_usage: Talk at C++Now 2025 and CppCon 2025; slides are in boostcon/cppnow_presentations_2025 (PDF) and CppCon/CppCon2025 (Keynote)
tradeoffs: Per the slides the final kernels are hand-written assembly, so the 'C++' result depends on inline assembly and an x86 AVX2/FMA target. Only the double-precision square-matrix case is shown.
caveats: No repository found: the author's GitHub profile (aliaksei-sala) lists only a conan-center-index fork, the CppCon 2025 repo holds slides only, and the slides give no code link, so has_code=false and the entry is reference-only. The 'beats OpenBLAS on Ryzen 9 9950X' numbers (1.70 vs 1.58 TFLOPS) are from a search-result snippet of a Medium post (medium.com is egress-blocked, YouTube also blocked): snippet only, unverified, and the slides I did open show OpenBLAS ahead (154.1 vs 142.2 GFLOPS) on the i5-6300HQ. Sala's authorship is Aliaksei Sala on the talk pages and 'salo.alexey' on Medium. Keep only as a lead: if a repo turns up, re-verify.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch '"faster than MKL" OR "faster than OpenBLAS" I implemented matrix multiplication C++ library blog post 2025 2026' surfaced the Medium post 'Achieving Peak performance for Matrix Multiplication in C++ !!!'; a follow-up WebSearch found the C++Now 2025 / CppCon 2025 talk titles; slides opened from the boostcon/cppnow_presentations_2025 repo.

name: LoopVectorization.jl
baseline: Intel MKL dgemm (single-threaded, via Julia LinearAlgebra.mul!)
workload: Float64 matrix multiply C = A*B with M=191, K=189, N=171, written as a plain triple loop under the @turbo macro, single thread, BenchmarkTools minimum time.
claimed_speedup: README example: @turbo triple-loop gemm minimum 111.722 microseconds (110.5 GFLOPS) vs MKL mul! minimum 117.221 microseconds (105.3 GFLOPS), about 5% faster (derived from page data); the same loop with only @inbounds @fastmath took 4.891 ms (about 44x slower than @turbo, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Julia (version not stated) with the @turbo macro; MKL selected with BLAS.set_num_threads(1) and BLAS.vendor() == :mkl.
tradeoffs: Julia only, not callable from C++ without embedding Julia. It is a loop-vectorizing macro, not a BLAS: @turbo reorders loops, does no bounds checking (misuse can segfault), supports only simple loop nests, and does no cache blocking or packing, so the README says parallelism and cache efficiency are left to the user and the gemm kernel suits small to medium matrices.
caveats: Single-shape, single-thread micro-benchmark with a margin of about 5%; the CPU is not named (README says 'the CPU I'm running these benchmarks on', Float64 SIMD width 8, which implies AVX-512). The README points to documentation benchmarks versus Julia, Clang, icc, ifort, gfortran and Eigen at JuliaSIMD.github.io, which is egress-blocked and was not opened. The package is in maintenance mode under the SciML small-grants programme. Julia-only, so it fits the 'then any' language filter rather than C++. Larger-size Julia work with this approach is Octavian.jl (already catalogued).
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Show HN BLAS library matrix multiplication faster than OpenBLAS MKL Eigen new open source' (HN domain filter) returned a thread whose snippet mentions LoopVectorization and Octavian.jl beating OpenBLAS/MKL; the repo README was opened on github.com and via raw.githubusercontent.com.

name: chgemm
baseline: gemmlowp (int8 GEMM); also reported against the fp32 single-core peak of the same CPU
workload: Single-core int8 x int8 to int32 symmetric-quantised GEMM on a Rockchip RK3399 (aarch64) core, row-major, built with -O3.
claimed_speedup: tpoisonooo/how-to-optimize-gemm README: chgemm int8 reaches up to 18.6 GFLOPS on one RK3399 core, against an fp32 single-core theoretical limit of 14.3 GFLOPS and 'gemmlowp about 12-14 GFLOPS' (roughly 1.3x to 1.55x vs gemmlowp, derived from page data). The chgemm README repeats 18.6 GFLOPS on RK3399 and about 23 GFLOPS on one AWS A72 core.
compiler_and_flags: -O3 (RK3399 build, per chgemm README); compiler name and version not stated; ARM assembly microkernels.
hardware: Rockchip RK3399 single core; AWS Cortex-A72 single core (about 23 GFLOPS, per chgemm README)
stars_or_usage: 68 stars; the how-to-optimize-gemm README says chgemm was merged into ncnn's INT8 convolution
tradeoffs: aarch64/ARM only, int8 inputs restricted to [-127, 127] (symmetric quantisation, -128 not allowed), int32 output, row-major, simplified C = A*B without alpha/beta, open packAB interface for deep-learning use. It is not a general BLAS replacement.
caveats: The gemmlowp number is an unsourced approximate range ('about 12-14 GFLOPS') in the README of a different repo (the tutorial how-to-optimize-gemm, GPLv3, 757 stars); no gemmlowp version, flags or shapes are given, and the peak 18.6 GFLOPS is a best case. GFLOPS here count int8 operations, so comparison with fp32 libraries is not like-for-like. Baseline gemmlowp is not one of OpenBLAS, MKL, Eigen or BLIS. Last commit June 2020. The same tutorial repo also shows a CUDA kernel above cuBLAS on an RTX 3080 as a graph with no numbers; not reported separately (GPU, off-baseline, no numbers).
found_via: Blogs / talks: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/gemm?l=c listed flame/how-to-optimize-gemm; the README of the related tpoisonooo/how-to-optimize-gemm tutorial (which links to a Zhihu blog post, blocked) points to chgemm.
